To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) term co‐occurrences in a database can be used to identify terms that are likely to be similar in meaning to the terms in a given query, (b) these similar terms are often frequent terms, and (c) frequent terms tend to be weak discriminating terms.

(1) the similar terms that are added to a user query by a cooccurrence query expansion system tend not to be good discriminators of relevance, and (2) this is because the terms that are identified tend to occur very commonly in the database.

1) the terms that are most similar to the terms specified in a user’s original query tend to occur frequently throughout the database that is searched by that query, and 2) terms that occur frequently in a document database tend not to discriminate well between relevant and non-relevant documents.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the limitations of cooccurrence data for use in query expansion systems.
the limitations of term cooccurrence data as a basis for identifying terms that are likely to be relevant to the original query statement.
the question of why query expansion based on term cooccurrence data often fails to improve retrieval effectiveness.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
term co‐occurence data is not a useful source of terms for query expansion.
the effectiveness of term co‐ occurrence data for query expansion is very limited indeed.
term cooccurrence data is of little use for query expansion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
term cooccurrence data is a poor indicator of term similarity for query expansion in a document retrieval system.
term cooccurrence data can be used for query expansion, but only when the cooccurrence data is based on documents that are very similar in topic to those in the database being searched.
cooccurrence data should not be used for query expansion.
The main takeaway from our work is that
query expansion systems should avoid adding terms that have a high probability of occurring in nonrelevant documents.
query expansion based on term cooccurrence data is likely to be of little or no value in most document retrieval applications.
cooccurrence data is not a reliable basis for query expansion, at least not when it is used as a basis for adding indexing terms that occur frequently in the document database.
